EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The programme contributed to long-term impact through ecosystem protection and restoration, improved forest management, and the adoption of nature-based solutions.

WWF FINLAND 2025

In 2024, the programme demonstrated strong progress in advancing inclusive conservation, climate adaptation, and sustainable natural resource governance across key landscapes in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. By the end of the third programme year, most planned outputs and outcomes had already been achieved. At the programme level only one indicator; trend in levels of Human Wildlife Conflict incidents, is not progressing in the desired direction. This suggests that while the programme is highly effective, future phases may require more ambitious target setting to match the pace and potential of implementation.

Finnish and international fora, raising awareness on the interconnectedness of biodiversity loss, climate change, and global security.

The programme contributed to long-term impact through ecosystem protection and restoration, improved forest management, and the adoption of nature-based solutions. These interventions have enhanced ecological connectivity and built resilience to climate change, while supporting the well-being of local communities and right holders.

The Mid-Term Review affirmed the programme’s strategic direction and Theory of Change, while also recommending stronger partner engagement on issues such as business planning and sustainability of restoration efforts. The programme’s flexibility, including unallocated budget use, and a long-term partnership approach remain key strengths in a volatile global context marked by funding cuts and rising environmental risks.

The programme’s policy advocacy and civil society support have become increasingly impactful. They have played a growing role in national and international discussions, linking local realities with global processes related to climate, biodiversity, and environmental security. This has been supported by strong communications work and strategic partnerships across sectors. WWF Finland has also solidified its role as a credible environmental voice in

However, some cross-cutting challenges remain. Gender imbalance and slow progress in disability inclusion highlight the need for deeper integration of equity and inclusion principles in programme delivery. In addition, political instability, administrative changes, bureaucratic delays, and shifting government priorities in some partner countries underscore the importance of adaptive management and maintaining active relationships with authorities.

Overall, the programme has proven capable of delivering measurable impacts while navigating complexity. As the end of the programme approaches, there is an opportunity to reflect critically on targetsetting, sustainability mechanisms, and how to best scale up locally led solutions in a globally challenging operating environment.

Partners reporting to the impact level indicator “Population trend of priority species” are Nepal and East Africa Wildlife Crime Hub (EAWCH). In 2024 there were no censuses of priority species conducted in Nepal. Rhinoceros populations in Kenya and Tanzania are increasing; 1059 black rhinoceroses in Kenya and 212 in Tanzania were reported in the year. There are no new numbers available for the elephant populations in 2024. Poaching of both the rhinoceros and the elephant have been decreasing in the region, with two rhinoceroses poached in Kenya and less than 20 reported elephant poaching cases in the region. On an impact level, the forest cover change for 2024 was not analysed against the programme specific indicators. This will be done at the end of the four-year programme. Globally, forest cover and deforestation trends regarding the year 2024 were not reported by the Global Forest Watch before this report was prepared. Of the programme partner countries and areas, Madagascar was able to reduce the deforestation rate in the programme landscape. This can be credited to strong efforts for capacity-building for community members related to conservation and forest management, reinforced and improved patrols and surveillance as well as awareness-raising. In Laos the deforestation is continuing at a high rate mostly due to the massive expansion of cassava plantations, which was very clearly observed during a monitoring visit to Laos. Also in Bolivia, severe deforestation continues as a result of land clearing incentives from the government as well as the expansion of soy production. In addition, massive forest fires destroyed large areas of forest in Bolivia during 2024 estimated covering between 11 and 14 million hectares, exceeding the last vast fires in 2019 figure by 90 percentage. In the Indonesian programme areas of Borneo and Papua deforestation has been stable but in other areas of the country deforestation

rates have again risen. In Tanzania, Uganda and Nepal the deforestation rates have been stable and in some instances forest cover has even increased in the programme areas. The programme has developed and implemented nature-based solutions (NbS), such as wetland and forest restoration e.g. through agroforestry and climate smart agriculture, as well as sustainable forest management, which provide climate adaptation benefits either as their main target or as an indirect benefit for people and nature. Although the nature-based, or adaptation, solutions are not yet at scale and concentrate to advanced solving of the local societal challenges in the face of climate change, the outcome results so far demonstrate that there has been a good uptake of NbS and adaptation interventions and thus still has future impact potential also at scale. In reference to cases of improved socio-economic status, there is no data for 2024, as the programme will conduct end line surveys of the socio-economic wellbeing surveys in the coming year. The target for people benefitting from climate activities under the programme has been exceeded and stands at 132% of the original goal, with 36,300 people reached. Throughout the year, a total of 22,737 right holders benefited from climate adaptation and NbS in the programme areas. Of the above 39% were women, 9,5% indigenous people, 1,6% PWDs and 1,6% youth. A total of 1,912 duty bearers were capacitated in 2024 on adaptation and NbS.

Climate-smart agricultural practices through mixed farming techniques, terrace usage and improved spice farming, alongside promoting eco-cultural tourism were adopted in Tanzania. Uganda enhanced climate resilience of the programme communities by implementing agroforestry, riverbank stabilization measures as NbS approaches supported by grey infrastructure enhancements and adaptation measures, such as rainwater harvesting in areas prone to climate change exacerbated impacts.

In 2024, communities and local authorities adopted a range of NbS and adaptation measures to strengthen climate resilience, supported by collaborative development efforts. WWF Nepal continued to support government authorities and local communities in restoring degraded areas and floodplains by implementing climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction measures through NbS including low-cost bioengineering, check dams, fencing and plantations along embankments to enhance ecosystem resilience and mitigate flood risks for agricultural and forest lands, benefiting 1,308 households.

Through the programme’s support, several climate change adaptation plans were developed and officially adopted at various administrative levels, representing key progress in embedding adaptation strategies locally. For example, Africa Adaptation Hub played a key role in supporting the development of a local adaptation plan which was adopted in Mozambique for 12 coastal communities, in Bolivia climate adaptation was integrated into land use plans of two municipalities, and in Uganda a climate change adaptation plan was developed and adopted for two sub-counties. In addition, Africa Adaptation Hub contributed to WWF’s engagement

at the global climate negotiations at the UNFCCC COP29 by inclusion of a key adaptation/NbS request in the WWF Africa COP29 Expectations Paper, aligning with global adaptation priorities. In Laos, climate adaptation activities had not commenced in full by the end of 2024 due to delays in the acceptance of the MoU. Implementation is scheduled for 2025. Uptake of climate adaptation measures has steadily increased throughout the programme’s implementation, among both communities and authorities. In 2024, a total of 33 adaptation plans and NbS initiatives received support under the programme. Demand for climate change adaptation has continued to grow, creating new opportunities across regions. Africa Adaptation Hub, together with WWF offices and partners, played a key role in advancing adaptation interventions, capacitybuilding, and regional advocacy. Meanwhile in Bolivia, significant efforts were made to strengthen the capacity of municipalities in climate adaptation and fire management, with successful

approaches already being replicated elsewhere. These developments have contributed to surpassing the targets set for this programme output. Implementation of NbS and adaptation interventions goes hand in hand with capacity building and skills development. Throughout 2024, the programme supported both rights holders and duty bearers in enhancing the adaptive capacities of communities, CSOs, and government counterparts. Through the Papua programme, WWF Indonesia assisted the Sundoy clan in drafting a management plan aimed at conserving forest and marine ecosystems within their ancestral lands. The area under traditional stewardship covers 9,921.87 hectares. A training on NbS for adaptation for WWF staff and CSO partners from Kenya, Uganda, Madagascar, Tanzania, and Somalia was convened as a joint effort by Africa Adaptation Hub and Voices for Just Climate Action (VCA) Alliance in Kenya. Also, CSOs and Pan-African youth networks (from Kavango-Zambezi, Greater Virunga Landscape and Southwestern Indian Ocean landscapes, as well as Kenya and Mozambique) were capacitated by Africa Adaptation Hub to enhance their influence on climate adaptation and natural resource governance and equipping them to integrate climate resilience strategies into their work. In Madagascar, CSO representatives and regional decision-makers received training on climate change challenges and policy strategies in order to strengthen their role in regional adaptation planning and advocacy. Similarly in Nepal, municipality authorities from seven municipalities were trained on climate change, disaster risk reduction and environment-friendly planning and the programme contributed to a partnership and project development between the International Federations of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and WWF Nepal. A series of training activities and workshops were held in Bolivia to capacitate both local civil society representatives, such as cocoa producers, livestock farmers, indigenous peoples’ representatives, people with disability and government authorities and technicians in forest fire prevention and management, as well as emergency response and inclusive management. Climate related decision-making processes influenced and climate financing leveraged through advocacy

The Africa Adaptation Hub also contributed to WWF’s position for climate COP negotiations.

WWF FINLAND 2025

In 2024, a total of 12 climate-related decisionmaking processes were influenced through programme efforts. At the regional level in Africa, climate advocacy was advanced through the Adaptation Hub, which operates as a key partner of the African Wildlife Foundation (AWF) in promoting climate adaptation and the role of protected areas. One major engagement was the Hub’s participation in the African Protected Area Directors (APAD) Conference, which brought together over 150 stakeholders including protected area directors, government officials, youth representatives, civil society organisations, private

sector actors, donors, NGOs, and representatives of Indigenous Peoples and local communities. As a result of this engagement, a five-year MoU was signed between APAD and AWF. The memorandum aims to enhance the contribution of Africa’s protected and conservation areas to global biodiversity and climate goals. With support from the programme, the Adaptation Hub will provide technical assistance for implementing the climate adaptation component of this agreement. The Africa Adaptation Hub also contributed to WWF’s position for climate COP negotiations by coauthoring the WWF Africa Expectations Paper for COP29. This document was widely disseminated across multiple platforms and formally presented to the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), helping to amplify WWF’s message, align with AGN priorities, and influence the COP29 negotiation outcomes. In addition, the Hub organised four side events at COP29, focusing on key themes including adaptation finance, NbS, climate–biodiversity

integration, and innovative financing mechanisms for Protected and Conserved Areas (PCAs). The Hub also developed and launched a policy brief together with the WWF network on “Enhancing Adaptation in NDC: Analysis and Reflections from 19 African countries” to inform on the development of a strong adaptation component in the next round of nationally determined contributions (NDC 3.0) for 2025. The analysis highlights that while many countries acknowledge climate risks, gaps remain in locally led adaptation, monitoring and evaluation and alignment with national adaptation plans (NAP), and emphasizes the need for increased adaptation finance, clear financial indicators, and stronger safeguards against maladaptive practices, in order to enhance resilience and long-term sustainability. Additional financial audit in Uganda In late 2023 WWF Finland commissioned an additional financial audit to WWF Uganda covering Finland’s support in calendar years 2020-2022. WWF Finland has previously considered this form of additional auditing and decided to initiate it in Uganda, the programme’s largest partner with an annual budget of EUR 350,000–400,000. The exercise included several lessons learned which are separately documented and summarised below:
• Define and confirm the timeline for the audit with the partner office taking into account possible holidays and negotiate if there are changes on the timeline. Make sure that relevant staff in the audited office are available during the time of the audit.
• Clearly specify the scope, number and nature of visits.
• Discuss and agree on the publicity of the audit report in the very beginning of the exercise.
• WWF Finland must submit the report to the primary donor (MFA) and they must submit all correspondence with the development aid receivers upon request to any interested party (Act on the Openness of Government Activities).
• Ensure that the engagement during the audit enables all parties to be updated on the process and understand where possible delays are caused.
• On the procurement of the service:
• We only received one quote. There must be enough time for the procurement process so that the service providers have time to submit a bid. WWF Finland was not able to get recommendations from other Finnish NGOs or network partners. Explore more efficient ways of distributing the request for quotations.
• Direct procurement by WWF Finland may lead to double VAT liabilities; both domestically and in the programme country. A potential mitigation measure could be to explore joint procurement arrangements with the audited WWF Office.
• Local auditors were cost effective and flexible.
